title: Project Structure
description: Understand the structure of an ASP.NET Core Web API project.

data.text: Understanding the **project structure** of an ASP.NET Core Web API helps you navigate, debug, and extend your code with confidence. Modern .NET uses a **host model** with a single `Program.cs` entry point that wires everything together — a big improvement over the older `Startup.cs` pattern.

In this lesson you will tour the typical files generated by `dotnet new webapi --use-controllers`, learn how the **middleware pipeline** processes them, and see exactly what each line of `Program.cs` does.

terms.definition: The object that boots your application, configures services, and runs the web server.
Dependency Injection container — holds the registered services your app can ask for via constructor parameters.
A component in the request pipeline that can inspect or transform an HTTP request (or short-circuit it).
The fluent builder created in `Program.cs`. You use it to register services (`builder.Services`) and configure the app (`builder.Configuration`, `builder.Logging`).
The built app. You use it to register middleware (`app.Use...`) and map endpoints (`app.MapControllers()`).

data.text: The default `Program.cs` generated by the controller template looks like this. Each region has a clear purpose.

data.title: Program.cs (controller template)
data.content: Annotated entry point for a controller-based Web API.

rows: Creates the host and loads configuration from `appsettings.json`, env vars, and command-line args.
Registers the MVC services needed to discover and run controller classes.
Required for the controller template; replace with `AddEndpointsApiExplorer` only if you go Minimal.
Adds metadata so endpoint-aware tools (Swagger, health checks) can introspect routes.
Needed for Swagger and minimal endpoints.
Pairs with `UseSwagger()` / `UseSwaggerUI()` to expose the docs UI.
Adds middleware that 307-redirects HTTP requests to HTTPS.
Skip in pure dev environments or behind a TLS-terminating proxy.
Adds the authorization middleware to the pipeline.
Required before `MapControllers()` if you use `[Authorize]` attributes.
Maps controller actions to routes based on their attributes.
Where the URL → action mapping happens.
Starts the web server and blocks until shutdown.

data.text: Every request flows through a **chain of middleware** in the order they were registered. Each component can do work *before* calling the next one, *after* it, or *instead of* it (short-circuit).

data.caption: Order of middleware in a typical ASP.NET Core Web API pipeline.
data.definition:
flowchart TB
    A[Incoming request] --> B[HTTPS Redirection]
    B --> C[Exception Handler]
    C --> D[Routing]
    D --> E[Authentication]
    E --> F[Authorization]
    F --> G[Controllers]
    G --> H[Outgoing response]
    H -.exception.-> C

data.title: Order is everything
data.text: Middleware runs in the order it is added. `UseAuthorization()` must come **after** `UseAuthentication()`, and `UseExceptionHandler()` should be registered **first** so it can wrap everything downstream.
As your API grows, you will add more folders. Here is a sensible structure for a real-world controller-based API.

data.caption: Recommended folder layout for a medium-sized Web API.
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[src/MyWebApi/] --> B[Controllers/]
    A --> C[Models/]
    A --> D[Services/]
    A --> E[Data/]
    A --> F[Dtos/]
    A --> G[Middlewares/]
    A --> H[Program.cs]
    A --> I[appsettings.json]

rows: Plain C# classes that represent domain entities.
Mirror your database tables, but never expose them directly.
Data Transfer Objects shaped for the wire (request/response contracts).
One DTO per use case; never reuse an entity as both.
Easy to unit test without spinning up a host.
Only this layer should know about the database.
Use sparingly — prefer filters or endpoint conventions when possible.

data.text: Modern .NET 8+ supports two styles in the same project. Pick whichever fits the size of your team and the size of your API.

cards.title: Controllers
cards.description: Classes with attributes that handle HTTP requests. Default in the `--use-controllers` template.
pros: Filters, model binding, and validation all 'just work'
Easy to organize dozens of endpoints
cons: Slight learning curve for attribute conventions

cards.title: Minimal APIs
cards.description: Endpoints defined inline in `Program.cs` with `app.MapGet(...)` and friends.
cons: Filters and validation need more wiring as the project grows

data.title: You can mix them
data.text: It is perfectly fine to register controllers with `AddControllers()` and *also* add minimal endpoints with `app.MapGet(...)`. The two styles live side by side inside one WebApplication.

data.title: Can you point to these in your project?

items.text: Where the middleware order is set.

data.title: Trace a request through your pipeline
data.description: Reading the code is not enough — describe the flow in your own words.
steps: Open `Program.cs` and list every middleware registered between `var app = builder.Build()` and `app.Run()`.
For each middleware, write one sentence describing what it does.
Run the API and hit `/weatherforecast` to confirm the pipeline is wired correctly.
Re-order `UseAuthorization()` to be **before** `UseHttpsRedirection()` and try to start the app — note the warning or behavior, then revert the order.
data.expectedOutcome: You can list the middleware in the correct order and explain why HTTPS redirection must run early. You can articulate how a request flows from `app.Run()` all the way back to a controller action.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `Program.cs` is the single entry point: build services, configure middleware, map endpoints, run.
`WebApplicationBuilder` registers services; `WebApplication` builds the middleware pipeline and route table.
Middleware order matters — register them in the correct sequence or authentication and authorization will silently fail.
A clean folder layout (Controllers, Models, Dtos, Services, Data) keeps concerns separated and tests easy.
Controllers and Minimal APIs can coexist — pick the style that matches the project's size and team familiarity.
data.takeaway: Modern ASP.NET Core boots from one file. Master `Program.cs` and you master the entire request lifecycle.
